title: "Tool 2.5 — Gaussianize First, Then Neutralize"
subtitle: "Straighten the proxy before you remove it"

```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd() / "src"))
from lectures import plotting, datasets  # noqa: F401
from lectures.plotting import INK, COOL, WARM, CRASH, despine, annotate_box  # noqa: F401
from lectures.gaussianization import gaussianize_1d
from lectures.measures import cka_linear, cka_rbf, mutual_information_xy, linfoot_r

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import pearsonr, spearmanr
```

*Learn-the-tool track · Lab 2.5.*

This lab climbs the **gaussianize-then-neutralize ladder** — one two-step recipe,
four datasets.  The [CKA penalty](lab-tool2-cka-penalty.qmd) removed a *curved*
leak by paying for a kernel.  Here we remove the same kind of leak with a *cheaper*
move: **straighten each feature into a Gaussian first, then run plain linear
neutralization on it.**  The reason it works is exact — a linear neutralizer can
only erase the *line* between a feature and $S$; gaussianizing a skewed proxy that
always moves in the same direction as $S$ turns the curved path by which $S$ leaks
into that feature *into* that line, so the cheap removal now reaches what it could
not before.  The *recipe* (gaussianize → neutralize) is built
once on Rung 1 and reused unchanged; only the **data grows up under it**, from a toy
whose leak you can see by hand to the real income basket.

**What you will produce:** an accuracy–fairness frontier (a curve showing the best
fairness reachable at each level of accuracy) showing that gaussianize-first
*dominates* plain neutralization — that is, it offers a strictly better deal: the
same accuracy at a smaller gap between groups — wherever the proxy carries $S$
through a continuous channel that always moves in the same direction with $S$.

---

## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer

Start where the leak is built by hand.  $S$ is the sensitive attribute and `x_leg`
is a legitimate feature independent of it.  The trap is `proxy` $= S^3$: it is a
**monotone** function of $S$ — it always moves in the same direction as $S$, so
knowing the proxy pins down $S$ almost exactly.  A rank-based measure (one that only
cares about ordering, like Spearman) therefore sees the dependence in full.  Yet
because the cube stretches the tails, a single regression *line* through
`(S, proxy)` leaves a large curved leftover (residual).  The
target genuinely rides on $S$, so a flexible model that keeps the proxy both **pays
off and leaks**.

```{python}
#| label: data-toy
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000

S: Float[Array, "n"] = rng.normal(0, 1, n)            # sensitive attribute  S ~ 𝒩(0,1)
x_leg: Float[Array, "n"] = rng.normal(0, 1, n)        # legitimate feature, ⟂ S

proxy: Float[Array, "n"] = S**3 + 0.2 * rng.normal(0, 1, n)   # proxy = S³ + ε   (monotone in S, but curved)
y: Float[Array, "n"] = 0.7 * x_leg + 0.6 * S + 0.3 * rng.normal(0, 1, n)   # y = 0.7·x_leg + 0.6·S + ε

print(f"spearman(proxy, S) = {spearmanr(proxy, S)[0]:+.3f}   (monotone — rank sees it fully)")
print(f"linear  CKA(proxy, S) = {cka_linear(proxy, S):.3f}   ← the line a neutralizer can erase")
print(f"kernel  CKA(proxy, S) = {cka_rbf(proxy, S):.3f}   ← the real dependence, curve and all")
print("the gap between them is the curvature linear neutralization cannot reach")
```

**The recipe — gaussianize each feature, then neutralize.**  Every rung below runs
exactly these three pieces, unchanged:

```
model_predict(Z)  = RBF-feature ridge on features Z      # flexible auditor: re-finds any leak
neutralize(F, S)  = F − [1, S] · lstsq([1, S], F)        # erase the LINE between each column and S
gaussianize → neutralize:  neutralize( Φ⁻¹∘rank (F), S ) # straighten first, THEN erase the line
```

The auditor is a random-Fourier-feature ridge — flexible enough to re-extract any
$S$-leak left in its inputs.  The neutralizer is the plainest possible fairness
move: fit the best straight line predicting each feature from $S$ and subtract it
off (residualize), which removes only the straight-line part of the dependence.
Gaussianizing is the one extra step, and the whole claim is that it changes *what
the line can catch*.

```{python}
#| label: toolkit
N_RFF = 400   # number of random Fourier features


def model_predict(Z: Float[Array, "n d"], y: Float[Array, "n"]) -> Float[Array, "n"]:
    """RBF-feature ridge — flexible enough to exploit any residual S-leak in Z."""
    Z = Z.reshape(-1, 1) if Z.ndim == 1 else Z
    Z = (Z - Z.mean(0)) / (Z.std(0) + 1e-9)            # standardize cols → auditor stable across scales

    r = np.random.default_rng(1)
    W: Float[Array, "d rff"] = r.normal(0, 1.0, (Z.shape[1], N_RFF))   # random projection
    b: Float[Array, "rff"] = r.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, N_RFF)            # random phase

    proj: Float[Array, "n rff"] = einx.dot("n d, d rff -> n rff", Z, W)   # Z·W
    phi: Float[Array, "n rff"] = np.cos(proj + b) * np.sqrt(2 / N_RFF)    # φ(z) = √(2/D)·cos(Z·W + b) ≈ RBF features

    gram: Float[Array, "rff rff"] = einx.dot("n i, n j -> i j", phi, phi)   # Φᵀ·Φ  (Gram matrix)
    rhs: Float[Array, "rff"] = einx.dot("n rff, n -> rff", phi, y)          # Φᵀ·y
    w: Float[Array, "rff"] = np.linalg.solve(gram + 1e-2 * np.eye(N_RFF), rhs)   # w = (ΦᵀΦ + λI)⁻¹·Φᵀy
    return einx.dot("n rff, rff -> n", phi, w)         # ŷ = Φ·w


def neutralize(F: Float[Array, "n d"], s: Float[Array, "n"]) -> Float[Array, "n d"]:
    """Linear neutralization: residualize each column of F on [1, s].

    Removes Fⱼ's straight-line component in s:  Fⱼ ← Fⱼ − [1, s]·(least-squares fit).
    A line is all it can erase — any curve in the Fⱼ↔s relationship survives.
    """
    A: Float[Array, "n 2"] = einx.rearrange("n, n -> n (1 + 1)", np.ones_like(s), s)   # design [1, s]
    out = np.empty_like(F)
    for j in range(F.shape[1]):
        coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, F[:, j], rcond=None)        # βⱼ = argmin‖A·β − Fⱼ‖²
        fit: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.dot("n p, p -> n", A, coef)   # A·βⱼ  (the line in s, p = [1, s] columns)
        out[:, j] = F[:, j] - fit                                 # Fⱼ − A·βⱼ   (part s cannot linearly explain)
    return out


def gaussianize_cols(F: Float[Array, "n d"]) -> Float[Array, "n d"]:
    """Φ⁻¹∘rank each column → standard normal marginals (monotone, per-feature)."""
    cols: Float[Array, "d n"] = np.stack([gaussianize_1d(F[:, j]) for j in range(F.shape[1])])
    return einx.rearrange("d n -> n d", cols)
```

Now train the auditor on three feature sets and audit each prediction's leak onto
$S$ — read with the **kernel** CKA and the histogram-based mutual information (how
much knowing $\hat{y}$ tells you about $S$), because the leak is curved and a linear
check would wave it through.  We report that mutual information on the **Linfoot R**
scale (MI rescaled to $R \in [0,1]$, which equals $|\rho|$ for a Gaussian, so it
sits on the same scale as CKA and the correlations and the three columns are
directly comparable):

```{python}
#| label: toy-audit
X: Float[Array, "n 2"] = einx.rearrange("n, n -> n (1 + 1)", x_leg, proxy)   # [x_leg, proxy]

runs = {
    "drop S, keep proxy": X,
    "linear-neutralize": neutralize(X, S),                       # plain Tool-1 move
    "gaussianize-FIRST, then neutralize": neutralize(gaussianize_cols(X), S),
}

print(f"{'representation':36s}{'acc R²':>8}{'CKA(ŷ,S)':>10}{'info R':>9}")
print("-" * 63)
toy_rows = {}
for name, Z in runs.items():
    p: Float[Array, "n"] = model_predict(Z, y)                   # auditor's prediction ŷ
    acc = max(pearsonr(p, y)[0] ** 2, 0.0)                       # accuracy = R²(ŷ, y)
    cka = cka_rbf(p, S)                                          # kernel CKA(ŷ, S) — curved leak
    mi = mutual_information_xy(p, S)                             # I(ŷ; S)   [nats]
    info_r = linfoot_r(mi)                                       # MI on the bounded [0,1] Linfoot scale (= |ρ| for a Gaussian)
    toy_rows[name] = (acc, cka, info_r)

    flag = "  ← leak gone" if cka < 0.02 else ""
    print(f"{name:36s}{acc:>8.2f}{cka:>10.3f}{info_r:>9.3f}{flag}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-toy-compute
# Gaussianize both axes, then fit the line a neutralizer would erase, in each frame.
gp: Float[Array, "n"] = gaussianize_1d(proxy)            # Φ⁻¹∘rank (proxy)
gS: Float[Array, "n"] = gaussianize_1d(S)                # Φ⁻¹∘rank (S)

panels = []
for fx, fy, ttl in [(S, proxy, "raw:  proxy = S³  vs  S"),
                    (gS, gp, "gaussianized:  Φ⁻¹(proxy)  vs  Φ⁻¹(S)")]:
    coef = np.polyfit(fx, fy, 1)                          # β = argmin‖fy − (β₀ + β₁·fx)‖²  (the line a neutralizer fits)
    xs: Float[Array, "n_grid"] = np.linspace(fx.min(), fx.max(), 50)
    line: Float[Array, "n_grid"] = np.polyval(coef, xs)   # β₀ + β₁·xs
    panels.append((fx, fy, ttl, xs, line))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-toy
#| fig-cap: "Why gaussianizing first lets the cheap neutralizer win. Left: the raw proxy S³ against S is a steep curve — a single regression line (red) fits it badly, so linear neutralization on the raw feature leaves most of the dependence behind. Right: after gaussianizing, the same relationship is nearly a straight line, so the very same linear neutralizer now erases it. The recipe does not add power to the removal; it reshapes the feature so the removal's one trick — erasing a line — is enough."
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))
for ax, (fx, fy, ttl, xs, line) in zip((axL, axR), panels):
    ax.scatter(fx, fy, s=8, c=COOL, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
    ax.plot(xs, line, c=CRASH, lw=2, label="linear fit (what gets erased)")
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
    despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The known answer holds.  Plain linear neutralization barely dents the leak
(CKA $0.13\!\to\!0.10$) — the line it erases is a poor fit to the cube, so the
auditor re-finds the curve.  Gaussianizing first collapses the leak to
CKA $\approx 0.02$, because $\Phi^{-1}\!\circ\text{rank}$ turns the monotone cube
into a near-straight line that the *same* neutralizer now removes whole.  The price
is visible in the accuracy column ($0.87\!\to\!0.62$): the $S$-derived signal goes
with the leak.  That is the recipe; now feed it a market.

---

## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market

$\text{proxy}=S^3$ never appears on a desk.  What *does* appear is a feature that
**tracks a group on a lopsided scale**: small for most people, with a long upper tail
that lines up with the protected group.  Think of a credit limit, a trading profit
(P&L), or an income figure.  `datasets.fair_regression()` supplies a legitimate
feature, a sensitive $S$, and a target that leans on $S$.  To it we attach exactly
that kind of proxy — a cubic, heavy-tailed channel from $S$ — and a target whose
useful signal also moves with $S$, so removing $S$ costs us real accuracy.
**Same `model_predict`, `neutralize`, `gaussianize_cols` — no new code.**

```{python}
#| label: data-rung2
d = datasets.fair_regression(n=600, seed=0)
x_leg2: Float[Array, "n"] = d["x"]                                 # legitimate feature
S2: Float[Array, "n"] = d["s"]                                     # sensitive attribute
rng2 = np.random.default_rng(2)

proxy2: Float[Array, "n"] = S2**3 + 0.5 * S2 + 0.25 * rng2.normal(0, 1, len(S2))   # proxy = S³ + ½·S + ε   (skewed, monotone leak)
y2: Float[Array, "n"] = 0.6 * x_leg2 + 0.9 * np.sign(S2) * np.sqrt(np.abs(S2)) \
    + 0.3 * rng2.normal(0, 1, len(S2))                            # y = 0.6·x_leg + 0.9·sign(S)·√|S| + ε   (signal rides on S)

X2: Float[Array, "n 2"] = einx.rearrange("n, n -> n (1 + 1)", x_leg2, proxy2)   # [x_leg, proxy]

print(f"spearman(proxy, S) = {spearmanr(proxy2, S2)[0]:+.3f}   (monotone — gaussianizing will straighten it)")
print(f"linear CKA(proxy, S) = {cka_linear(proxy2, S2):.3f}  vs  kernel CKA = {cka_rbf(proxy2, S2):.3f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: rung2-audit
print(f"{'representation':36s}{'acc R²':>8}{'CKA(ŷ,S)':>10}{'info R':>9}")
print("-" * 63)
r2_rows = {}
for name, Z in {"drop S, keep proxy": X2,
                "linear-neutralize": neutralize(X2, S2),
                "gaussianize-FIRST, then neutralize": neutralize(gaussianize_cols(X2), S2)}.items():
    p: Float[Array, "n"] = model_predict(Z, y2)                  # auditor's prediction ŷ
    acc = max(pearsonr(p, y2)[0] ** 2, 0.0)                      # accuracy = R²(ŷ, y)
    cka = cka_rbf(p, S2)                                         # kernel CKA(ŷ, S)
    mi = mutual_information_xy(p, S2)                            # I(ŷ; S)   [nats]
    info_r = linfoot_r(mi)                                       # MI on the bounded [0,1] Linfoot scale (= |ρ| for a Gaussian)
    r2_rows[name] = (acc, cka, info_r)

    flag = "  ← leak gone" if cka < 0.02 else ""
    print(f"{name:36s}{acc:>8.2f}{cka:>10.3f}{info_r:>9.3f}{flag}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-rung2
#| fig-cap: "The stylized market, three feature sets. Each bar pair reads accuracy (R², orange) against the prediction's residual dependence on S (CKA, blue→red). Dropping S and plain linear neutralization sit at the same high CKA — the cheap removal cannot reach the cubic proxy, so it buys almost no fairness. Gaussianize-first collapses the bar to ≈0 by giving up the S-derived accuracy: it is the only column that actually moves the group leak, and the trade is now explicit."
labels = list(r2_rows)
accs = [r2_rows[k][0] for k in labels]
ckas = [r2_rows[k][1] for k in labels]
ypos = np.arange(len(labels))[::-1]

fig, (axA, axC) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4), sharey=True)
axA.barh(ypos, accs, color=WARM)
axA.set_title("accuracy  R²(ŷ, y)", fontsize=12)
axA.set_yticks(ypos)
axA.set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=10)
axC.barh(ypos, ckas, color=[COOL if c < 0.02 else CRASH for c in ckas])
axC.axvline(0.02, color=INK, ls="--", lw=1)
axC.set_title("leak  CKA(ŷ, S)  ·  lower = fairer", fontsize=12)
for ax in (axA, axC):
    despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read the two pictures together.  *Dropping* $S$ and *linearly neutralizing* land at
the **same** high CKA — the proxy's cube defeats a line, so the cheap removal is
spending effort for nothing.  Only gaussianize-first moves the leak, and it pays for
it in accuracy ($0.83\!\to\!0.43$): the part of the signal that was really $S$ in
disguise is gone.  Nothing in the recipe changed — only the data — yet the lesson is
sharper, because now the accuracy you trade away is a number a desk would feel.  On
to a basket where the proxies are real.

## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket

Now the real panel.  We **reload** the prepared ACS (American Community Survey)
income data — there is no cleaning here; the Census decode, the income label, the
protected attribute, and the proxy matrix all live in
[the income & fairness dataset primer](../../data/06-the-credit-dataset.qmd) — split
it into the standard $(X, y, s)$, and run the *same* recipe.  The one lab-local step
is **encoding the categoricals** (turning each category into 0/1 indicator columns,
"one-hot", for `occupation` and `marital`), our modelling choice; the numeric proxies
(`age`, `education_years`, `hours_per_week`) are what gaussianizing acts on.

**What we are looking for here:** we predict who earns over \$50k, then measure how
much the prediction still leaks the protected attribute `sex`.  The key number is the
prediction's leak onto `sex` — read as CKA, and on the same scale as info R — and the
question is whether gaussianizing the numeric proxies first lowers it on *real* data,
or whether the leak lives somewhere the recipe cannot reach.

```{python}
#| label: real-load
import pandas as pd

credit = datasets.load_credit()                                   # prepared ACS panel + target
y_r: Float[Array, "n_all"] = credit["income_high"].to_numpy().astype(float)   # target: 1 if income > $50k
s_r: Float[Array, "n_all"] = credit["sex"].to_numpy().astype(float)           # protected: 1 = male
Xdf = credit.drop(columns=["income_high", "sex"])                 # proxies — sex DROPPED
print(f"{len(credit):,} rows · proxies: {list(Xdf.columns)}")
print(credit.head(3).to_string(index=False))

# the only lab-local step: subsample for the O(n²) kernel audit, one-hot the categoricals
rng_r = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = rng_r.choice(len(credit), 1800, replace=False)              # kernel CKA builds n×n — subsample
credit_s = credit.iloc[idx].reset_index(drop=True)
y_r, s_r = y_r[idx], s_r[idx]

num = ["age", "education_years", "hours_per_week"]                # gaussianizing acts on these
cat = ["occupation", "marital"]                                  # one-hot — our modelling choice
Xnum: Float[Array, "n 3"] = credit_s[num].to_numpy().astype(float)
Xcat: Float[Array, "n d_cat"] = pd.get_dummies(credit_s[cat], drop_first=True).to_numpy().astype(float)

Xr: Float[Array, "n d"] = np.column_stack([Xnum, Xcat])          # feature block = [numeric | one-hot]
print(f"\nfeature matrix: {Xnum.shape[1]} numeric + {Xcat.shape[1]} one-hot columns")
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Where This Data Comes From
The Census decode, the `income_high > $50k` target, the protected attribute `sex`,
and the proxy matrix (with `sex` dropped) are all built and owned **once** in
[The Income & Fairness Dataset](../../data/06-the-credit-dataset.qmd).  This lab
reloads that prepared $(X, y, s)$ and never re-derives the decode or the ACSIncome
filter; the only lab-local step is one-hot encoding the categoricals and a subsample
for the kernel audit.  That primer also shows *where the leak hides*: chiefly in
`occupation`, which is heavily sex-segregated.
:::

The recipe runs unchanged — gaussianize only the numeric proxies (a monotone
per-feature map; one-hot indicators are already $\{0,1\}$ and have nothing to
straighten), then neutralize the whole block against $s$ and audit:

```{python}
#| label: real-audit
def gaussianize_numeric(F: Float[Array, "n d"], k: int) -> Float[Array, "n d"]:
    """Gaussianize the first k (numeric) columns; leave the one-hot tail as-is."""
    cols: Float[Array, "d n"] = np.stack(
        [gaussianize_1d(F[:, j]) if j < k else F[:, j] for j in range(F.shape[1])]
    )
    return einx.rearrange("d n -> n d", cols)


print(f"{'representation':30s}{'acc R²':>8}{'CKA(ŷ,s)':>10}{'info R':>9}")
print("-" * 57)
real_rows = {}
for name, Z in {"drop sex, keep proxies": Xr,
                "linear-neutralize": neutralize(Xr, s_r),
                "gaussianize-FIRST": neutralize(gaussianize_numeric(Xr, len(num)), s_r)}.items():
    p: Float[Array, "n"] = model_predict(Z, y_r)                 # auditor's prediction ŷ
    acc = max(pearsonr(p, y_r)[0] ** 2, 0.0)                     # accuracy = R²(ŷ, y)
    cka = cka_rbf(p, s_r)                                        # kernel CKA(ŷ, sex)
    mi = mutual_information_xy(p, s_r)                           # I(ŷ; sex)   [nats]
    info_r = linfoot_r(mi)                                       # MI on the bounded [0,1] Linfoot scale (= |ρ| for a Gaussian)
    real_rows[name] = (acc, cka, info_r)

    print(f"{name:30s}{acc:>8.2f}{cka:>10.3f}{info_r:>9.3f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-compute
# Per-numeric-proxy monotone leak onto sex, plus the categorical (occupation) leak the recipe can't touch.
sp = pd.Series({c: spearmanr(credit_s[c], credit_s["sex"])[0] for c in num}).sort_values()   # ρ_S(proxy, sex) per column

occ_male = credit_s.groupby("occupation").sex.transform("mean")   # P̂(male | occupation)
occ_guess = (occ_male > 0.5).astype(int)                          # majority-sex guess per occupation
occ_leak = (occ_guess == credit_s.sex).mean()                    # accuracy = mean(guess == sex)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-real
#| fig-cap: "Where gaussianize-first pays off on real data — and where it cannot reach. Each numeric proxy's monotone leak onto sex (spearman, bars) is the channel gaussianizing straightens; hours-per-week carries the most, age almost none. But the dashed line marks the dominant leak the recipe leaves untouched: occupation, a categorical, recovers sex about 65% of the time on its own. Marginal gaussianization only straightens continuous features, so on the real basket the residual group dependence lives in the channel it structurally cannot touch."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 3.0))
ax.barh(sp.index, sp.values, color=[GREEN if abs(v) < 0.1 else COOL for v in sp.values])
ax.axvline(0, color=INK, lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("spearman(proxy, sex)  ·  the monotone channel gaussianizing straightens")
ax.set_title(f"Numeric leaks are weak; occupation (categorical) recovers sex {occ_leak:.0%} — untouched",
             fontsize=11)
despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The honest reading: on real ACS data the prediction's leak onto `sex` is already
**small** (CKA $\approx 0.02$), and gaussianize-first acts only on the weak numeric
channels.  So it cannot drive the leak to zero here, because the biggest leak comes
from `occupation` — a **categorical** feature (named job groups, not a number) that
recovers `sex` about $65\%$ of the time on its own.  Gaussianizing one feature at a
time can only straighten *continuous* proxies, so it has no grip on a categorical.
This is the recipe's one boundary, now in the wild: it wins exactly when a skewed
proxy that always moves with the group, and is *continuous*, carries that group — and
tells you, by the leftover leak, when a different tool
is needed.  To see the win at full strength we return to a market where that
assumption holds and trace the whole trade-off.

---

## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — The Frontier vs Plain Neutralization

The deliverable is an **accuracy–fairness frontier**.  We dial the removal from
"keep the leak" to "fully neutralized" and, at each setting, plot accuracy against
how much the prediction still depends on the group, for **plain neutralization**
(Tool 2's linear move) versus **gaussianize-first**.  We run the sweep on the Rung-2
market — where the proxy is a continuous, skewed channel that always moves in step
with $S$, the exact case gaussianize-first is built for.  To trace the curve we mix
each pipeline's leaky prediction with its fully neutralized one in steadily growing
amounts.

**What we are looking for:** whether the gaussianize-first curve *dominates* the
plain one — sits at a smaller group gap for every level of accuracy.  If it does, the
recipe gives you a fairness option the plain move simply cannot offer.

```{python}
#| label: frontier
def frontier(Z_leaky: Float[Array, "n d"], s: Float[Array, "n"],
             y: Float[Array, "n"]) -> tuple[Float[Array, "t"], Float[Array, "t"]]:
    """Trace (accuracy, CKA) as the removal blends from leaky → fully neutralized."""
    p_leak: Float[Array, "n"] = model_predict(Z_leaky, y)         # neutralize OFF
    p_neut: Float[Array, "n"] = model_predict(neutralize(Z_leaky, s), y)   # neutralize ON

    accs, ckas = [], []
    for t in np.linspace(0, 1, 9):                            # blend weight t: 0 keep leak, 1 neutralize
        p: Float[Array, "n"] = (1 - t) * p_leak + t * p_neut  # ŷ(t) = (1−t)·ŷ_leak + t·ŷ_neut
        accs.append(max(pearsonr(p, y)[0] ** 2, 0.0))         # accuracy = R²(ŷ(t), y)
        ckas.append(cka_rbf(p, s))                            # leak = CKA(ŷ(t), S)
    return np.array(accs), np.array(ckas)


acc_plain, cka_plain = frontier(X2, S2, y2)                   # plain: raw features
acc_gauss, cka_gauss = frontier(gaussianize_cols(X2), S2, y2)  # gaussianize-first

print(f"plain neutralization : CKA floor = {cka_plain.min():.3f}  (cannot go below — the curve survives)")
print(f"gaussianize-first    : CKA floor = {cka_gauss.min():.3f}  (the leak is reachable now)")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-frontier
#| fig-cap: "The accuracy–fairness frontier: gaussianize-first (green) dominates plain neutralization (red). Plain neutralization is a near-vertical stub — sweeping the removal barely moves CKA off ≈0.30, because a line cannot erase the cubic proxy, so you cannot buy fairness at any accuracy. Gaussianize-first sweeps a full curve from the same accurate-but-leaky corner down to CKA≈0, trading accuracy for neutrality on real terms. At every CKA target the green curve offers an option the red one cannot reach: the recipe is strictly better wherever the proxy leaks through a continuous monotone channel."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.4))
ax.plot(cka_plain, acc_plain, "-o", c=CRASH, lw=2.2, label="plain neutralization (Tool 2)")
ax.plot(cka_gauss, acc_gauss, "-o", c=GREEN, lw=2.2, label="gaussianize-first (Tool 2.5)")
ax.annotate("plain stalls —\nline can't reach the curve",
            (cka_plain.mean(), acc_plain.min()), textcoords="offset points",
            xytext=(8, -28), fontsize=9, color=CRASH)
ax.annotate("dominating frontier",
            (cka_gauss[4], acc_gauss[4]), textcoords="offset points",
            xytext=(10, 8), fontsize=9, color=GREEN)
ax.set_xlabel("CKA(ŷ, S)  →  less neutral")
ax.set_ylabel("accuracy (R²)")
ax.set_title("Gaussianize-first dominates the plain-neutralization frontier", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9.5, frameon=False, loc="lower right")
despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

There it is: a frontier you can choose a point on.  Plain neutralization gives you
**no choice** — its sweep is a vertical stub pinned at CKA $\approx 0.30$, because
the line it erases never fits the cubic proxy, so the group leak survives at every
accuracy.  Gaussianize-first opens the whole trade-off: from the same accurate-but-
leaky corner it sweeps down to CKA $\approx 0$, dominating the plain frontier at
every level.  The win is not magic — it is the Rung-1 mechanism at scale: straighten
the monotone proxy and the cheap linear removal suddenly reaches the dependence it
could never catch raw.

That is the full climb: the same gaussianize-then-neutralize recipe removed a toy
cube, a stylized market proxy, and the continuous channels of a real income basket —
escalating only the data, never the recipe, and ending on a dominating frontier.
Its one boundary, seen on Rung 3, is the categorical leak no marginal map can
straighten; when that is the dominant channel, the [CKA penalty](lab-tool2-cka-penalty.qmd)
removes the dependence directly, kernel and all, and the [adversarial
remover](lab-tool3-adversarial.qmd) learns it from data.
